newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines' Ramos again says he wants to retire.
newsitem.headline: Philippines' Ramos again says he wants to retire.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos, long tipped as a closet candidate for the 1998 presidential election despite a constitutional ban on a second term, has again denied he wants to stay in the top job.
"I do not seek another term and will not seek it...I graduate in June 1998, period," Ramos told a dinner on Friday night.

A private petition, which claims to have more than five million signatures, is aimed at trying to overturn the ban on a president serving more than one six-year term so Ramos can seek re-election next June.

Analysts have repeatedly suggested the former general has been quietly engineering a second term and warned it could polarise a society only just returning to normal after the dictatorship of Ferdinand Marcos.
While Ramos said he sympathised with attempts to change the constitution, an end to the ban on a second term would anyway come too late for him to stand in the next election.
At a news conference in Manila last week, Ramos said that after June 1998 he wanted to enjoy his retirement.
The constitution was rewritten 10 years ago after Marcos fled the country, and included the presidential term limit with Marcos specifically in mind.
Ramos is widely seen as having presided over one of the most successful periods of Philippine history, with sustained economic growth and political stability.
At least a dozen candidates are already jockeying for front position to replace him and Ramos has invited all to go on brief "presidential courses" to get a feel for the job.
At the moment the most popular candidate is vice-president, and opposition party member, Joseph Estrada.
However, while the former action movie hero is hugely popular among the masses, he is widely distrusted by the business community who question his economic knowledge.
